      "body": "I have a few issues with CloudFlare:\r\n\r\n# Problem with CloudFlare\r\nCloudFlare is a vigilante extremist organization who takes the decentralized web and centralizes it under one corporate power that controls the worlds largest walled-garden. A very large portion of the web (10%+) that was once freely open to all is now controlled and monitored by one central authority who decides for everyone who can see what web content. This does serious damage to net neutrality, privacy, and has immediate serious consequences:\r\n\r\n* Cloudflare has a policy to block all Tor users by default. It's a crude, reckless and unsophisticated (but cheap) way to create the illusion of security. [Collateral damage is high](https://blog.torproject.org/trouble-cloudflare). Privacy takes a global hit because Cloudflare has decided what best suits their business to the detriment of everyone else.\r\n* The damage to anonymity helps spy orgs conduct illegal surveillance. The consequential access inequality constitutes a network neutrality abuse. Access equality is central to net neutrality.\r\nCloudFlare is a man-in-the-middle who sees all traffic including tunneled HTTPS traffic (and thus raw unhashed passwords!).\r\n* No transparency: as Cloudflare performs a DoS attack on Tor users they obviously do not inform web owners. Web owners are usually unaware that legitimate patrons are being blocked from accessing their site. These businesses are all damaged so that one business can profit.\r\n* Cloudflare [shields criminal webmasters](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2015/nov/19/cloudflare-accused-by-anonymous-helping-isis) by hiding their IP address from the public. A website involved with crime often has other criminal websites on the same IP, but users who try to protect themselves cannot block the IP address of the malicious site.\r\n* Cloudflare makes heavy use of CAPTCHAs which triggers many ethical problems: \r\n   * Google's reCAPTCHAs [compromise](https://cryptome.org/2016/07/cloudflare-de-anons-tor.htm) anonymity.\r\n   * CAPTCHAs put humans to work for machines when it is machines who should be working for humans.\r\n   * The CAPTCHAs are often broken.\r\n   * The CAPTCHAs often require the user to execute non-free javascript.\r\n   * Tor users are driven off of Tor because CloudFlare creates such a hostile environment for them that it becomes impractical to deal with all the CAPTCHAs.\r\n   * The CAPTCHAs entail a connection to **PRISM** corp *Google*, giving Google Inc. an opportunity to collect data, abuse it, and profit from it.  E.g. Google can track which of their logged-in users are visiting the page presenting the CAPTCHA.\r\n   * The CAPTCHAs block *all* robots indiscriminately causing collateral damage to good (non-malicious) robots.\r\n   * GUI CAPTCHAs deny service to users of text-based web browsers. \r\n E.g. CloudFlare's GUI CAPTCHA breaks `torsocks lynx 'https://www.simplyrecipes.com/recipes/buffalo_wings/'`.  CloudFlare effectively dictates that all Tor users must use a GUI browser and in many cases it must also be javascript capable.\r\n* Cloudflare is potentially [injecting javascript spyware](https://crimeflare.com/) into the traffic of their patrons to collect data (this is how cloudflare pays their bills).\r\n* CloudFlare [deceives](http://cryto.net/~joepie91/blog/2016/07/14/cloudflare-we-have-a-problem/) website visitors into believing their connection is secure (HTTPS & browser padlock) when in fact the user is MitMd.\r\n\r\n# Suggested actions\r\n* Document a guideline for reviewers to consider whether a tool relies on or forces users into CloudFlare's walled-garden.  It may be over the top to have all CloudFlare relationships trigger condemnation of the tool but it should at least be a strong factor.\r\n* When a recommended app forces CloudFlare on users in any context, there should be a loud and clear anti-feature showing.  Specifically, projects for these two recommended apps force users seeking a support page into CF:\r\n   * Wire (https://github.com/wireapp/wire-webapp/issues/5716)\r\n   * Signal\r\n"

      "body": "Since my previous comment, I have migrated from Cloudflare to Gandi LiveDNS (my registrar). It's not entirely painless process, but here are the general steps:\r\n\r\n1. Disable DNSSEC at Cloudflare and Gandi if it was enabled. Cloudflare will say that they will disable it when the records are removed from Gandi who will recommend you to **not change your DNS servers for 72 hours!**\r\n    * I don't know if this is actually necessary, but I didn't find that much instructions on how to transfer DNS with DNSSEC enabled domain and decided that the safest route is disabling DNSSEC at the old provider and enabling it on the new one.\r\n2. Export your DNS zone in advanced DNS settings at Cloudflare.\r\n3. Import the zone to Gandi by editing some parts by hand (SOA and especially TTLs). Cloudflare will have TTLs set to 1 for domains with DDoS protection and Gandi's minimum is 300. This confused me, because Gandi only gave unclear error messages, but I have sent them feedback.\r\n4. Restore DNSSEC as Cloudflare isn't the only one providing one-click-DNSSEC anymore :purple_heart: \r\n\r\nIn case of IPFS, I changed my IPFS gateway variables from cloudflare-ipfs.com to ipns.co ([GitHub repo](https://github.com/VanVan/ipfsProxyHTTP))."

      "body": "We are off CloudFlare. Hopefully we don't take *too* much of a performance hit. Try it out! https://www.privacytools.io/"

      "body": "Subjecting visitors to CF is worse than subjecting them to bad performance. PTIO is promoting them, the least they can do is serve their own branded logos.\r\n* Any images that can't be linked to external sites could be isolated to a separate PTIO host.       "author": "Participant 13",
      "body": "Image dimensions is something I’ll work on today, I *think* we’re mostly good on that but there are definitely a few that need those specified. \r\n\r\nI don’t really think we should use third parties to host our images. With the current solution we can guarantee that there’s no access logging for web visitors. \r\n\r\nWhen I say we took a performance hit, it wasn’t that bad. Of course there was going to be a difference between a single server in Germany vs a network of hundreds of servers internationally serving our content, but we do have a high performance server and like you said, I think the trade-off was worth it to move off CloudFlare. \r\n\r\nI’m pretty happy with the results so far :)\r\n\r\nWe have our own Searx instance now, I’ll probably just link to that or a list of public instances once we get ours listed in more places. \r\n\r\nRegarding everything else, probably best if you open a separate issue for them, like PayPal.   "title": "❌ Software Removal | github",
  "body": "# Drop Github, avoid Gitlab, endorse notabug.org\r\n\r\nSince PTIO was reorganized it's unclear if github is being endorsed.  There is no mention in the productivity category but the *participate* page links to github.  PTIO is leading by poor example in this case.  It's embarrassing to the project and not good for credibility.  Luckily it no longer appears on the front page.\r\n\r\nBefore continuing, it's worth mentioning that Github and Gitlab both distribute the free software that implements their service.  Unless I say otherwise, this post is about their *service*, not their software.\r\n\r\n## Privacy problems with Microsoft Github *service*\r\n\r\n1. MS feeds other privacy abusers:\r\n   1. Github uses Amazon AWS which triggers [several privacy and ethical problems](https://github.com/wireapp/wire/issues/265)\r\n   1. (2012) MS spent $35 million on Facebook advertisements, making it the third highest financial supporter of a notorious privacy abuser that year.\r\n1. Censorship and PTIO project interference: Github staff apparently [deleted](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/374#issuecomment-468537031) a PTIO contributor who was reporting a privacy abuses present on other projects.  Hostility toward volunteer privacy advocates working for PTIO is in itself sufficient reason to abandon Github.\r\n1. Github may have a policy that entails censoring bug reports (see [this post](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/763#issuecomment-482189305) for the discussion)\r\n1. Github is Tor-hostile ([according to Tor project](https://trac.torproject.org/projects/tor/wiki/org/doc/ListOfServicesBlockingTor#ComputingTechnical), although personally I've had no issue using Tor for GH) \r\n1. MS is a PRISM corporation prone to mass surveillance\r\n1. MS lobbies for privacy-hostile policy:\r\n   1. MS supported CISPA and CISA unwarranted information exchange bills, and CISA passed.\r\n   1. (2018) MS [paid](http://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1401518&view=late1&session=2017) $195k to [fight privacy in CA](https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2018/04/facebook-donated-200000-to-kill-a-privacy-law-but-now-its-backtracking/)\r\n1. MS supplies Bing search service which gives high rankings to [privacy-abusing](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/374#issuecomment-460077544) CloudFlare websites.\r\n1. MS supplies hotmail.com email service, which uses vigilante extremist org *Spamhaus* to force residential internet users to share all their e-mail metadata and payloads with a corporate third-party.\r\n1. MS drug tests its employees, thus intruding on their privacy outside the workplace.\r\n1. MS products (Office in particular) violate the GDPR\r\n1. To report an MS security bug, one must sign in and the [sign-in page](https://msrc.microsoft.com/create-report) is broken.  It's really bad for security to make defect reports difficult to submit.\r\n\r\n### Privacy-compromising consequence of using Github for the PTIO project:\r\n1. (conflict of interest) PTIO selects only contributors willing to make privacy compromises, and excludes those who will not use GH for privacy reasons.\r\n1. (conflict of interest) When contributors are evaluating whether a tool is privacy-respecting, they white list Microsoft and Amazon as a consequence of PTIO using Github, and then [use that](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/779#issuecomment-473503845) as rationale to endorse an unworthy tool.\r\n1. (side-effect) Privacy advocates who use GH face demoralizing criticism for what some regard as hypocrisy.  PTIO contributors should not be subjected to that.\r\n\r\n## Rationale for staying with Github:\r\n1. The shake-up of making a move will lose contributors.\r\n1. *e-voting* was mentioned, but self-hosted GitLab probably supports this (the GL service does).\r\n\r\n## Problems with Gitlab *service*\r\n\r\nMany Github refugees fled to Gitlab when Microsoft acquired Github.  It's a [bad idea](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/742#issuecomment-481424035).  Gitlab should be avoided.\r\n\r\n## Alternatives\r\n\r\n1. self-hosting (Gogs, Gitea, Gitlab, etc.)\r\n   1. (+) avoids the \"shake-up\" problem of shrinking the community each time the project moves (there is no risk that the privacy factors would later take a negative turn).\r\n   1. (+) PTIO could host other privacy-focused projects and become part of the support structure for them.  Centralizing privacy-focused projects would increase PTIO visibility and establish a place where developers with the same high-level goals could develop in a more united way.  Poaching privacy-focused projects from GH and GL would solve the hypocrisy problem those projects are facing as well.\r\n1. Bitbucket\r\n   1. (-) dodgy j/s up the yin yang that [clusterfucks uMatrix](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/843#issuecomment-483830547)\r\n   1. (-) has some relationship with Netlify, who uses AWS\r\n   1. (-) non-free software?\r\n1. Launchpad\r\n1. notabug.org (\"NAB\") ([privacy policy](https://notabug.org/tos#Privacy)).  Based on a liberated fork of gogs.\r\n   1. (+) [supports Tor](https://notabug.org/tor) (although the *onion* web UI is currently disabled in response to attack, so the onion site only accepts git connections)\r\n   1. (+) supports SSH keys and SSH over Tor to NAB's onion service\r\n   1. (+) no CAPTCHAs\r\n   1. (+) registration very non-intrusive, and not controlling about where you get your email\r\n   1. (+) hosts Jeff Cliff's [CF-Tor](https://notabug.org/themusicgod1/cloudflare-tor) project which is one of the most credible and competently staffed privacy projects.  \r\n   1. (-) noteworthy drawback unrelated to privacy: e-voting non-existent.  Framadate.org could be used but probably quite inconvenient.\r\n   1. (-) drawback not related to privacy: NAB doesn't associate PGP keys to users, so PGP signed commits may be unavailable or more manual work needed.  I doubt that's a factor for PTIO.\r\n   1. (-) IRC support channel is dead.\r\n1. [Codeberg](https://codeberg.org/).  Runs on [Gitea](https://docs.gitea.io/en-us/), which is a Gogs fork.  [Suggested](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/338#issuecomment-483727853) by @izzysoft.\r\n   1. (+) web UI works on Tor (probably SSH as well)\r\n   1. (+) supports SSH and GPG keys\r\n   1. (+) no CAPTCHAs\r\n   1. (+) registration very non-intrusive, and not controlling about where you get your email\r\n   1. (+) functions without any j/s, and the javascript that exists is all 1st-party ([ref](https://github.com/privacytoolsIO/privacytools.io/issues/843#issuecomment-483830547))\r\n   1. (+) supports e-voting\r\n   1. (-) logins don't work from Ungoogled Chromium\r\n   1. (-) no onion address?\r\n\r\nI haven't made a significant effort to dig up dirt on these suppliers, but I can confirm that NAB has none of the issues of Github.  My experience with NAB has been quite positive.",

      "body": "I understand git, no worries on that score  ;-)   But the key thing about github is not the 'git' portion but rather the 'hub' portion. But there are other venues:  mastodon instance, matrix chatroom, self-hosted by privacy-respecting people.  Who are already cross-posting things brought up in those areas, here to github.  Mikaela just posted something from the matrixChatroom where somebody had suggested \"libre videogames\" listings.  JonahAragon posted something similar, which was from an email-conversation (which is Not An Official Way to contact the project-maintainers because it does not scale... so dear readership please do not use that mechanism... but it does function as a fallback option of last resort methinks).  \r\n\r\nThe main question is not, how many people will we attract if we selfhost a gitlab-instance that refuse to use github... the main question is, are there benefits to gitlabSelfhosting that are impossible to achieve on github + mastodonSelfhosted + matrixHomeserver + reddit + twitter + maybeFacebook + discourseSelfhosted + keybase + lastResortFallbackToEmail?       "body": "Perhaps, for a simple implementation, gitea could run an [ipfs](https://ipfs.io) node in the background hosting local repository files (using [ipns](https://docs.ipfs.io/concepts/ipns/) to point to the latest versions of the repositories).       "updated_at": null,
      "author": "Participant 8",
      "body": "> There is no requirement for peer-to-peer storage here\r\n\r\nI think gitea would benefit greatly from peer-to-peer sharing of repositories so that popular repos would be redundant in the case of instances going down. While someone can just mirror a repository to their own instance, it would fragment the development of a project if there is no central place to commit to. If the git protocol was layered on IPFS, it would allow for deduplication when forking projects on a single instance (so an entire copy wouldn't have to be stored). \r\n> what you describe doesn't seem required or even related to the problem at hand.\r\n\r\nThe reason federation is so useful (and why people want it so much) is that it allows collaboration across instances. The InterPlanetary Name System (IPNS) has identical behavior to OpenID because it can be used to identify a user who has permission to update certain data (e.g. their repositories and personal profile). An IPNS address could uniquely identify a user from another instance without necessarily having to tie that user to a specific instance. Lets give an example:\r\nAlice is self-hosting an instance of gitea at aliceland.net\r\nWhen Alice creates a new account, gitea would create an empty profile, host it on IPFS and then generate a unique IPNS address that points to that profile. Whenever Alice creates a new repository or updates her profile in any way, gitea will (behind the scenes) create a new IPFS record, unpin the old one, and reassign Alice's IPNS address to it.\r\nNow lets say Bob wants to submit a merge request from his mirror of the repository on bobland.net to aliceland.net.\r\nWhen Bob originally forked Alice's repo to bobland.net he made a note of the IPNS of Alice's repo as well as the IPFS location of the commit he forked from.\r\nWhen Bob wants to open a merge request, he writes his message and then bobland.net will put the following things in an IPFS block:\r\n- Bob's IPNS user address\r\n- The IPFS address of the commits Bob wants to pull in\r\n- The IPFS address of the commit in Alice's repo that should be modified\r\n- Bob's Messsage and Title for the merge request\r\n- Signature of data with Bob's private IPNS profile key\r\n\r\nBobland.net will then send the IPFS address to aliceland.net which can then choose to totally ignore it, OR parse the address, verify the commits, create a IPNS address for the comment thread (that points to all the comments) and then notify Alice that some guy named Bob on instance Bobland.net has sent a merge request for 3 commits over IPFS. The comments would also be hosted over IPFS and accessible via an IPNS address.\r\nThis pattern of using IPNS for mutable data (like a comment thread) and IPFS for immutable data (like comments and commits) can be applied for most inter-instance federation.\r\n>I don't think there's interest in moving away from the Git storage format and transfer protocol.\r\n\r\nThis approach to federation wouldn't have to move away from the Git format. [Git can simply be layered and stored on ifps](https://docs.ipfs.io/how-to/host-git-style-repo/) (while also taking advantage of deduplication). Git's Merkle Tree system doesn't necessarily have to be integrated with IPFS's (although that would be cool) and the git transfer protocol would still be the same, IPFS would just moderate the communication between instances."
